title: ABSTRACT
text:
High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising
technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at
bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advan-
tage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency,
out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the
accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance
and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space,
we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for het-
erogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-
level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior.
HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation,
and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a cal-
ibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of
Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that
differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does
not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; HBM is better
used to hold the running sequences’ KV cache than as a cache for
HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0
to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes.
The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim
and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Memory capacity has emerged as a primary bottleneck in serv-
ing large language models (LLMs). Model weights occupy tens to
hundreds of gigabytes, while key–value (KV) state grows linearly
with context length and request concurrency, quickly exceeding
accelerator memory capacity. For example, an 8B model serving
eight concurrent 128K-context sessions can exhaust the HBM of
a modern GPU (e.g., the 131 GiB of HBM3e on an NVIDIA H200),
while long-context serving for 70B-class models may exceed the
memory capacity of an entire eight-GPU node [5, 11, 17, 22]. High
Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising ap-
proach for extending accelerator-local memory capacity. SanDisk’s
disclosed HBF design targets a 16-die, 512 GB flash stack that deliv-
ers up to 1.6 TB/s [24, 25], enabling multi-terabyte accelerator-local
memory systems without host-memory accesses. The same disclo-
sure targets 8–16× HBM capacity at similar cost and bandwidth,
making capacity per dollar, rather than higher speed, the main
motivation for HBF [24].
Unlike conventional DRAM expansion, HBF brings asymmet-
ric read and write performance, page programming, flash transla-
tion layer (FTL) management, write amplification, and finite pro-
gram/erase endurance into the accelerator memory hierarchy. Its
effect on LLM serving is difficult to predict because no public HBF
hardware is available for validation [28]. Nevertheless, system archi-
tects must decide on memory organization, placement policies, and
provisioning before production devices become available. For ex-
ample, moving read-only weights to HBF mainly exercises its read

HBM+HBF memory hierarchies under realistic LLM serving work-
loads before committing to a design. Because such hardware is
unavailable, a simulator is required to evaluate these trade-offs.
Existing simulators each cover one level of this hierarchy: DRAM
simulators [14, 16] stop at the memory controller, SSD simula-
tors [13, 29] put flash behind a storage interface, and LLM serving
simulators [4, 10, 36] represent memory by capacity and bandwidth.
None connects the placement of LLM data to both completion time
and physical flash traffic.
HBFSim addresses this limitation. It models HBM, HBF with a
host-managed FTL, and conventional capacity tiers in one event
system, coupled in a closed loop with a serving frontend whose
scheduler and GPU compute are calibrated against measurements,
and it accepts address-level traces as well as production request
traces. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and
Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input
and output lengths. We find that HBF serves the data that does not
fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; that HBM should
hold the running sequences’ KV, because caching HBF with LRU or
FIFO rereads nearly the whole working set once it exceeds HBM,
and that KV should be written to HBF only when it must leave
HBM; and that the FTL costs little on the read path as long as its
layout keeps reads parallel, while HBF’s lifetime depends on the
amount of KV that reaches flash. These findings connect HBF’s
potential cost-per-bit advantage to measurable latency and wear
rather than to a single capacity or bandwidth number.
This paper makes the following contributions:
• Workloads at two granularities. HBFSim takes fine-
grained address-level traces, with one record per memory
access, and coarse-grained request traces, which its frontend
expands into the series of weight and KV accesses that each
request causes.
• A coupled and fast memory-system model. HBM, HBF
with a host-managed FTL, and external tiers (host DRAM,
CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs) share one timeline and interact
as in a real system, for example through the FTL’s tables in
HBM.
• Preliminary takeaways for HBF. Decoding Llama-3.1-
70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads yields
five simple rules: HBF pays off only under capacity pressure;
HBM should hold the running KV and HBF the weights, with
KV written to flash only when it must leave HBM; generic
cache replacement loses to this placement unless a step fits
in HBM with room to spare; the FTL should preserve the
flash array’s parallelism; and endurance, set by how much
KV reaches flash, is a first-order constraint.

title: BACKGROUND
text:
2.1
Memory Demand of LLM Serving
A serving system’s memory holds the model weights, which every
request reuses; the KV cache, the per-layer keys and values of every
processed token, which decoding reads instead of recomputing; and
activations, which are small by comparison. For Llama-3.1-70B a
BF16 KV cache takes 320 KiB per token [5], 320 GiB for 1M tokens.
Serving systems allocate KV in fixed-size blocks [11] and retain
the blocks of finished requests so that later requests with the same
prefix skip its prefill [22, 37], so the KV footprint grows beyond
the active requests. Figure 1 shows the weights and the KV cache
of 1M tokens, in one request or retained across many: for small
models the KV cache dominates, every model from 70B up exceeds
eight HBM4 stacks, and the newest open models, with 1.6T to 2.8T
parameters, exceed even an eight-H200 node with their weights
alone, while hybrid or compressed attention keeps their KV small.
The two phases of a request access this data differently. Prefill
processes the prompt, produces its KV, and is usually compute-
bound; chunked prefill lets it share a batch with decoding work [2].
Each decoding step generates one token per request: it reuses the
weights across the batch, reads every running request’s KV, and
appends one token’s KV per layer, so it is usually bound by memory
bandwidth, and its traffic grows with model size, batch, and context.
When weights and KV exceed HBM, systems offload to host DRAM
or SSDs [15, 22, 26], at access costs set by the slower tier and its
interconnect.
2.2
High Bandwidth Flash
HBF stacks NAND flash dies on a logic base die and connects them
to the accelerator through an HBM-like interface in the same pack-
age [24, 25]. The OCP HBF specification [19] defines stacks with
up to 16 channels and three speed grades. For example, at speed
grade 2 each channel carries 96 GB/s of payload, or about 1.5 TB/s
per stack, and SanDisk targets 512 GB per stack. An HBF stack
therefore offers 8-16 times the capacity of an HBM stack at a similar
interface bandwidth.
However, HBF still behaves like NAND. A page read takes mi-
croseconds, compared to tens of nanoseconds of DRAM, so HBF
reaches its bandwidth only with many reads in flight. Data is pro-
grammed, not overwritten: a page program takes tens of microsec-
onds and occupies its bank, and a block must be erased before its
pages are programmed again. The specification assigns address
mapping, garbage collection (GC), and wear leveling to host soft-
ware; the device itself performs neither GC nor copyback [19]. Each
block tolerates a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles,
and no P/E rating for HBF has been published. Host decisions thus
shape both performance and lifetime: what the host places in HBF

2.3
Questions for HBM+HBF Systems
Before HBF hardware is available, system designers need to answer
five questions. Is HBF a better capacity tier than host DRAM or
SSDs? How much HBM should accompany it? Which data should
stay in HBM, and should HBM act as a cache for HBF or as sepa-
rately addressed memory? How should the FTL handle KV writes?
How long will HBF last under serving traffic? The answers depend
on each other through the serving loop: slower memory stretches
decoding steps, which changes how requests are batched and there-
fore the memory traffic itself. Answering them requires running a
real serving scheduler against memory models that include flash
management, with the two coupled in a closed loop.
HBFSIM DESIGN
HBFSim is a closed-loop simulator of LLM serving on accelerator
memory built from HBM, HBF, and other capacity tiers. Figure 2
shows its three layers. A serving frontend turns request traces into
batches and the requests in each batch into memory accesses. A
policy layer decides in which memory each object is stored and how
data moves between tiers. A device engine executes the memory
transactions on models of HBM, HBF, or external capacity tiers,
and feeds the outcome of that work back to the frontend, which
schedules the next batch based on the feedback. Slower memory
therefore reshapes batching as it would on a real system: longer
iterations let more requests queue before the next one starts, and
when KV no longer fits, the scheduler moves some KV to a slower
tier or preempts requests, which shrinks the batch. Three challenges
shape this design.
Workloads and device accesses differ in granularity and
semantics. A serving system works with requests, weights, and KV
blocks; HBM serves data bursts of tens of bytes; and HBF is accessed
like memory but programs flash pages (e.g., 4 KiB) in order, erases
whole flash blocks, and leaves its FTL to the host. Address-level
traces preserve individual accesses but can only cover short runs,
whereas production request traces cover long periods of serving
but record no memory accesses.
The levels of the memory hierarchy are coupled. Existing
simulators model one level in isolation, but in an HBM+HBF sys-
tem the two levels jointly determine performance. What HBF must
serve depends on what HBM can hold, and the traffic HBF gener-
ates in turn consumes HBM capacity and bandwidth. Placement
decisions therefore shift load between the tiers rather than simply
adding a slower level beneath HBM, so neither tier can be simulated
independently.
The number of events is huge. One decoding step of a 70B
model reads tens of millions of flash pages, each passing through
about a dozen shared resources, from the plane and flash channel
to the TSVs and ECC engine. Because slower memory changes
batching, these accesses must be simulated in a closed loop rather
than replayed.
As shown in Figure 2, layers in HBFSim communicate through
narrow interfaces. The frontend describes work in terms of model
objects such as weight tensors and KV blocks. Policies map objects
to devices and emit transaction graphs with explicit dependencies.
The engine contains no LLM-specific logic. This separation lets
users change one layer, for example, add a caching policy or an
FTL, without touching the others.
3.1
Serving Frontend
HBFSim accepts workloads at two granularities. In an address-level
trace, a record is one memory access with optional data class, ar-
rival time, and layer annotations; such traces are replayed directly.
Detailed instruction-and-address tracing and cycle-level simulation
incur substantial costs even for a small inference workload. For
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (bfloat16, batch size 1), a 32-token prefill
followed by two fixed-token decode steps required 43.4 minutes for
trace collection on an RTX 4000 Ada with NVBit [30]. The resulting
1,030-kernel traces occupy 98.3 GiB uncompressed, or 7.46 GiB in
the compressed format consumed by Accel-Sim2.0 [20]. Full trace-
driven simulation already takes 19.9 wall-clock hours even for a
small model. For larger models, both the trace size and simulation
time would become prohibitively large, rendering this approach
unrealistic.
In a request-level trace, a record is one inference request: its
arrival time, prompt and output lengths, and prefix hashes [22, 31].
It contains no detailed memory accesses. Which bytes an inference
step touches does not depend on the values it computes, only on
the model architecture and on which requests the scheduler runs
with how many tokens (for MoE models, also on the routed experts,
which depend on the values and are therefore an input, recorded
or synthetic). The frontend, ServeLoop, therefore regenerates the
accesses of every step. Its scheduler replays the trace with vLLM’s
continuous batching and chunked prefill [2, 11, 35], including paged
KV, prefix sharing, and preemption. A compiler turns each iteration
into the byte ranges that every operator reads or writes in weight
tensors, KV blocks, and embedding rows, leaving addresses and
memories to the policies. A decoding step of Llama-3.1-70B under
the workload with 32 sequences and 6K tokens of context becomes
1.8 × 105 such transactions.
The generated accesses are verified at three levels. Batching:
given the same service times, the scheduler forms the same batches

match 6,568 held-out warp streams captured with NVBit on an

traffic is a lower bound.
HBFSim times every batch, prefill and decode alike, using an
operator-level GPU model. It decomposes each batch into opera-
tors and computes each operator’s time from three components: a
fixed overhead, a compute time, and a memory-access time. The
compute time is derived from the operator’s FLOPs and a compute-
throughput coefficient fitted to measured kernels. We obtain the
memory-access time from HBFSim’s detailed simulation of HBM
and HBF accesses, rather than an ideal-bandwidth assumption. To
stay anchored to real GPU behavior, we fit each operator’s fixed
overhead, compute throughput, and memory bandwidth from mea-
sured kernels to establish a baseline time. During simulation, we
replace the baseline’s ideal memory time with the simulated access
time, while retaining the measured kernel’s additional memory
overhead beyond the GPU’s peak bandwidth. The batch time is
then the sum of all operator times. This design ensures that HBF
latency and bandwidth directly affect each operator’s memory time,
and thus the batch time, while the compute portion stays tied to
measured GPU performance.
3.2
Memory Policies
HBFSim provides two ways to organize HBM and HBF. In peer
mode, HBM and HBF form one address space, and each object is
stored in one of them. HBM is filled in a priority order and the rest
overflows to HBF: weights first places the weights, then KV blocks
in address order, retained prefixes included; KV first places the
running sequences’ KV, then the weights, then the retained prefixes.
In tiered mode, HBM caches objects stored in the HBF or other
capacity tier in 4 MiB lines with LRU, FIFO, or decayed-LFU [23]
replacement; decayed LFU evicts the line with the fewest recent
accesses and halves all access counts periodically, as in frequency-
based replacement [23]. Dirty data is tracked at 4 KiB granularity,
and dirty KV is written back either eagerly, while compute leaves
the link idle [12], or only when its line is evicted. KV released before
eviction is discarded without being written.
3.3
Device Engine
HBM. An HBM stack follows the JEDEC organization of its gen-
eration, set by the number of channels and pseudo-channels and
the pin rate. The following study uses HBM4 for analysis [8], with
32 channels of two pseudo-channels at 8 Gb/s per pin, or 2 TB/s
per stack. Because our studies concern capacity tiers, HBFSim mod-
els HBM at the pseudo-channel level rather than at the command
level of DRAM simulators such as Ramulator 2.0 [16]. Requests are
split into pseudo-channel transfers, groups of four pseudo-channels
share an arbitration queue and a service timeline, and an average ac-
cess latency and a bandwidth efficiency account for row activation
and refresh.
HBF. As in the OCP specification, the model separates the device
from its host-side management. The device has independent trans-
mit and receive timelines for each channel, ordered page sensing
within each bank, page buffers, ECC, and TSV transfers. It programs
the pages of a block in order and, as the specification requires, erases
a block when its first page is written. The organization of flash into
channels, dies, planes, and blocks and the timing of reads, programs,
and erases follow MQSim [29]. We reimplemented them because
MQSim’s FTL runs inside an SSD, whereas HBF’s runs on the host,
and HBF operations must share one timeline with HBM and the
serving frontend. Like an SSD, and beyond the specification, each
stack has a device-managed DRAM that buffers writes until a page
is full and caches recently read pages. The host runs the FTL. It
maps logical pages to physical ones and runs garbage collection,
which picks victim blocks by their number of valid pages with
a small weight for wear; static wear leveling is implemented but
switched off in our studies. Since the specification forbids the device
from moving valid data, garbage collection reads live pages into a
copy buffer in HBM and writes them back. We implemented three
mappings and keep each one’s index in HBM. Page-level mapping
has an 8-byte entry per 4 KiB page; the whole table lives in flash as
translation pages, and HBM caches part of it. Extent mapping keeps
a sorted list of runs of consecutive pages, 48 B per run. Both write
by appending and spread consecutive pages over all planes. Block-
level mapping has one entry per 1 MiB logical block and keeps the
block in one physical block on one plane, each page at a fixed offset.
We model two consequences: NAND programs a block’s pages in
order, so a page whose predecessors have not been written yet
waits in the device DRAM; and any write that is not an in-order
append copies the whole block to a fresh one. We do not stripe
blocks over planes, because a copy would then move a 1.5 GiB stripe.
Every mapping gets 0.1% of the HBF capacity in HBM, 3.1 GiB of
the 96 GiB of two HBM4 stacks, and its lookups compete with the
application’s traffic: with page-level mapping, one Llama-3.1-70B
decoding step at 2 HBM + 6 HBF issues 1.0–1.7×107 lookups, one
per flash page read.
Other tiers. Host DRAM, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs share one
model consisting of a link, a controller, and media queues. A CXL
SSD adds a device-side DRAM cache with FIFO replacement.
3.4
Simulation Speed
To make full-iteration simulation tractable, we combine coarse-
grained HBM approximation with exact HBF acceleration. Only
HBM is approximated: scheduling transfers per 4 KiB chunk and
pseudo-channel rather than per 32-byte burst runs an all-HBM for-
ward pass 24.8× faster (134.7× for sequential reads), while keeping
batch completion times within 0.04%.
For HBF, the bottleneck is reserving roughly a dozen shared
resources per page, as in SimpleSSD [9]; here we reduce per-
reservation overhead without sacrificing accuracy. A first-fit calen-
dar organizes each resource’s idle intervals into 64-interval leaves
labeled with their maximum duration, so searches immediately
bypass leaves with insufficient space. Multi-page reads are batched
into groups of one page per plane to share stage-time calculations,
reuse calendar lookup states across groups, and compute stride
addresses from the first page, while the FTL updates free space
only for planes whose state changes. Page grouping speeds up

Calibration and Validation
Three components are calibrated against hardware (Figure 3a). The

same token ranges, prefix hits, and completion times. The operator
model is fitted to kernel measurements: on an A100 and an H200

attention that vLLM uses with 8-bit weights, inside whole layers
under CUDA graphs, over 525 shapes per GPU spanning batch,
query, and context sizes, and fitted each operator’s fixed overhead,
compute rate, and memory rate by least squares. We then predict
64 whole-layer shapes that never entered the fit: the mean absolute
error is 5.8% on the A100 and 5.0% on the H200, and the largest,
41.8% on the A100, occurs in Llama-3.1-70B layers whose batch
mixes long and short contexts. Finally we run complete requests on
each GPU, from the embedding to the output head, and compare
each batch’s time: predicted and measured batch times differ by
10.2% on average on the A100 (Llama-3.1-8B, 46 batches) and by
5.8% on the H200 (Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B, 86 batches);

the test suite compares HBM scheduling, HBF reads and writes, and
GC against reference models, and every result records the hashes
of its inputs, configuration, and binary.
CASE STUDIES
We use HBFSim to answer the questions of Section 2.3 with two
models and three workloads.
4.1
Setup
System. We model one accelerator package with eight memory
stacks, each an HBM4 stack or an HBF stack (Table 1); we write
2 HBM + 6 HBF for a package of two HBM and six HBF stacks
(2:6 in the figures, 2H6F in Table 3). We compare 1 HBM + 7 HBF,
2 HBM + 6 HBF, 4 HBM + 4 HBF, and 6 HBM + 2 HBF, whose HBM
holds 43.4, 91.9, 188.9, and 285.9 GiB of data. The HBF stacks follow

stack has a device DRAM of 0.1% of its flash that serves as write
buffer and read cache. Unless noted otherwise, the host FTL uses
page-level mapping and caches translation pages in 0.1% of the HBF

4.2
HBF Versus Other Capacity Tiers
At 2 HBM + 6 HBF with weights first, the capacity tier serves 38–
65 GiB of running KV per step for Llama-3.1-70B and 145–157 GiB
for Qwen3-235B-A22B, whose 223 GiB of weights exceed HBM:
115 GiB of weights and all 30–42 GiB of running KV. We keep this
placement and replace the six HBF stacks with host DRAM, a CXL
SSD, or an NVMe SSD of the same capacity (Figure 4a). HBF decodes
11.0–14.4× faster than host DRAM, 16.1–21.3× faster than the CXL
SSD, and 86.6–115.0× faster than the NVMe SSD for Llama-3.1-70B,
and 18.6–19.0×, 66.8–154.1×, and 150.3–154.1× faster for Qwen3-
235B-A22B. The step time is roughly the tier read divided by the
tier’s bandwidth: six on-package HBF stacks serve 157 GiB in 0.17 s,
PCIe-attached host DRAM in 3.2 s, and the NVMe SSD’s NAND
at 6.6 GB/s in 26 s. The CXL SSD’s device DRAM (5% of its flash,
153.6 GiB) holds the spill of Llama-3.1-70B and of the first two
Qwen3-235B-A22B workloads, so the CXL SSD stays within 1.5× of
host DRAM there; the 157 GiB spill of long INPUT exceeds it and
the CXL SSD is as slow as the NVMe SSD (26.0 s). We keep all 32
sequences in every system, so each tier serves the same spill; a real
system would shrink the batch.
An off-package tier occupies none of the package’s eight stack
sites, which can then hold HBM. Figure 4b therefore compares
seven systems on eight sites, all with KV first: 2 HBM + 6 HBF;
2 HBM with the HBF’s capacity off package as a CXL or NVMe SSD,
alone or behind 256 GiB of host DRAM (one accelerator’s share
of a 2 TiB server), leaving six sites empty; and 8 HBM with the
CXL SSD, alone or behind host DRAM. With two HBM stacks, the
weights that do not fit in HBM come from the tier in every step:
2 HBM + 6 HBF is 9.3–12.5× faster than 2 HBM + host DRAM +
CXL SSD for Llama-3.1-70B and 19.1–19.5× for Qwen3-235B-A22B.
Host DRAM holds the first 256 GiB of the tier, which covers both
models’ weights, so the SSD behind it is never read and the NVMe
and CXL variants coincide. The SSDs alone are 13.5–18.3× (CXL)
and 70.8–98.0× (NVMe) slower than 2 HBM + 6 HBF for Llama-3.1-
70B, and 66.9–99.3× and 154.3–157.2× for Qwen3-235B-A22B. With
eight HBM stacks (384 GiB), both working sets fit, no step reads the
off-package tier, and TPOT is 49–55 ms: 1.4–1.5× below 2 HBM +
6 HBF for Llama-3.1-70B and 2.9× below it for Qwen3-235B-A22B.
An off-package tier thus wins only when the sites it frees go to
HBM and the step fits in that HBM; then a cheap tier serves as well
as a fast one.
Takeaway 1: HBF is most valuable under memory-capacity
pressure. It offers little benefit when the working set fits in HBM,
but substantially outperforms offloading to CPU memory, CXL
SSDs, and NVMe SSDs once spilling occurs, for example when
Qwen3-235B-A22B serves 32 sequences whose 253–265 GiB work-
ing set exceeds the 188.9 GiB of HBM at 4 HBM + 4 HBF. Under
a fixed stack budget, however, adding more HBM can hurt per-
formance if the resulting loss of HBF bandwidth outweighs the
reduction in spill traffic.

per step from HBF (89–98 ms). Under long OUTPUT, weights first

whereas proactive migration creates avoidable writes for KV entries
that may be freed shortly.

allelism rather than maximize address granularity. Decode
reads weights and KV in long sequential runs, so one translation
serves many pages. An extent mapping that stripes each run across
all planes matches a page-level table at a fraction of its memory,
whereas a block-level mapping that keeps each block on a single
plane serializes its page reads and slows decoding considerably.

4.5
Which HBF Parameters Matter?
The HBF specification is still a draft, so we ask which device pa-
rameters the results depend on, taking Llama-3.1-70B on the three
workloads at 2 HBM + 6 HBF with KV first, where a step reads
29–49 GiB of weights from HBF (69–83 ms per token), and changing
one parameter at a time (Figure 9).
Only the rate at which the flash array senses pages matters.
Doubling the page read time to 8 𝜇s raises TPOT by 30–42%, 16 𝜇s
by 91–126%, and the 40 𝜇s of conventional NAND by 3.7–4.8×;
halving the planes per die at equal capacity has the same effect as
doubling the read time (29–40% for 8 planes, 87–121% for 4). The
interface does not matter: speed grade 3 doubles grade 2’s 1.5 TB/s
and changes TPOT by 0.1%, and grades 1 and 2 on 8 channels are
equally 29–40% slower, only because their stacks have half the
planes. A plane senses one 4 KiB page per read time, so a stack’s
256 planes deliver 0.26 TB/s at 4 𝜇s, a sixth of the interface. The
write side is invisible in decode, even without the device DRAM:
with KV first a step appends its KV in HBM and programs no HBF
page, so program times from 37.5 to 600 𝜇s, write credits, and write
timeout leave TPOT unchanged, and the thermal throttling ceiling
adds at most 0.2%. For read-heavy decode, an HBF design should
therefore spend on planes and read time before interface speed.

title: DISCUSSION
text:
Limitations. Our case studies reproduce one decoding step per
workload, seven tokens per running sequence, and one prefill win-
dow per workload for the write path and the mapping comparison,
without garbage collection, so TPOT omits its interference with
reads. We model one accelerator; tensor or pipeline parallelism
would give each a share of the weights and KV. The studies com-
bine an H200 compute profile, extended beyond its measured batch
of 16, with HBM4 and HBF, a pairing that does not exist today,
so HBF timing and endurance remain assumptions. The lifetime
estimates apply a published serving load around the clock to the
HBF write share and write amplification that HBFSim measures,
and assume perfect wear leveling.
Extending HBFSim. New memory policies use the policy in-
terface, new FTL schemes the host mapping interface, new HBF
generations the device configuration, and new models, traces, and
GPUs their descriptors, importers, or operator profiles.

title: RELATED WORK
text:
HBF and hybrid HBM–flash memory. H3 [7] and SK hynix [27]
evaluate hybrid HBM+HBF organizations with projected device
parameters. FlashAccel co-designs data layout and storage man-
agement for HBF [32]. Petrucci et al. compare HBF with LPDDR
analytically and identify writes as the limit for offloading KV to
flash [21]. HBFSim lets such designs be compared on the same
workloads; our endurance results quantify the write problem they
point out.
Memory and storage simulators. Ramulator 2.0 [16] and
DRAMsim3 [14] model DRAM at the command level. MQSim [29]
and FEMU [13] model SSDs behind an NVMe interface, with map-
ping, GC, and wear leveling inside the device, and Cylon [34] emu-
lates CXL SSDs with a DRAM cache in the device. HBFSim follows
MQSim’s approach to the flash organization and Cylon’s device
class for the CXL SSD, but treats HBF as memory with a host-side
FTL whose metadata competes with the application in HBM.
LLM serving simulators. Vidur [1], LLMServingSim [3], Fron-
tier [6], and ASTRA-sim [33] simulate scheduling, computation,
and communication for LLM inference, LLMCompass [36] adds
operator-level modeling with mapping search, and GTSim [4] and
Accel-Sim [10, 20] model GPU microarchitecture. They represent
memory by its capacity and bandwidth; HBFSim models the de-
vices at the transaction level, flash management included, under a
validated scheduler.

title: CONCLUSION
text:
HBF could give accelerators an order of magnitude more memory,
but only if systems use it in ways that suit flash. HBFSim lets
researchers test these choices before hardware exists. Our case
studies support five takeaways. HBF is most valuable under capacity
pressure, where it keeps TPOT 11.0–19.0× lower than host DRAM
and 86.6–154.1× lower than an NVMe SSD. Conventional cache
replacement is a poor fit for HBM–HBF tiering: no policy matches

Li et al.
peer mode with KV first once the set a step reads exceeds HBM,
and a cache wins only when that set fits with room to spare. HBM
should hold the running sequences’ KV and HBF the read-only
weights; KV should move to HBF only when it must leave HBM.
The mapping should preserve the flash array’s parallelism, which an
extent index does at a fraction of a page table’s memory. Endurance
is a first-order constraint: at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B,
HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share
the KV writes. We release HBFSim so that others can replace our
assumptions with measurements.
